## MAJOR-4 remote-half proof (session token over the SSH forward)

`start` minted/reused the session token on file, exported it to the remote worker's environment,
and every later command in the documented sequence (`status`'s probe, the live pytest, `measure`)
authenticated against `/health`, `/version` and `/ocr` with **no manual `export
PADDLE_WORKER_TOKEN=...` step**. `status` showed `probe.available: true` / `reason: "ok"`
immediately after `tunnel-up`, and `measure` completed 21 authenticated `/ocr` requests (1 cold +
20 warm, plus the `verify_identity` `/version` call before them) without a single 401.

rasterised to an image-only PDF at 300 dpi (the D5-pinned raster dpi) and re-encoded as PNG:

## What this measures (and does not)

This is the Paddle rung's cost per SYNTHETIC page at 300 dpi on an idle, already-deployed RTX
5090 worker over a warm SSH tunnel. It does not include: model download/first-install time (the
official PP-OCRv5 models were already cached on the host before this measurement — a fresh
instance would pay that cost once), Vast.ai instance provisioning/boot time, or any measurement
against the 13-document legal escalation population (D8: that population is not sent to Vast in
Phase 2.1).

## Commands run (host/port/user/token never shown; the runbook has the full sequence)

```
python -m tools.paddle_vast check
python -m tools.paddle_vast deploy
python -m tools.paddle_vast start
python -m tools.paddle_vast tunnel-up
python -m tools.paddle_vast status
PADDLE_REMOTE_OPT_IN=I_ACCEPT_REMOTE_PAID_PADDLE_OCR python -m pytest tests/test_paddle_live.py -m live -q
PADDLE_REMOTE_OPT_IN=I_ACCEPT_REMOTE_PAID_PADDLE_OCR python <the evidence_sha256 two-run stability probe, ad hoc, not committed>
python -m tools.paddle_vast stop && python -m tools.paddle_vast start   # fresh restart for a genuine cold measurement
PADDLE_REMOTE_OPT_IN=I_ACCEPT_REMOTE_PAID_PADDLE_OCR python -m tools.paddle_vast measure --n-rows 8 --warm-requests 20
python -m tools.paddle_vast stop
python -m tools.paddle_vast tunnel-down
```

Every one of the above (except the ad hoc probe, described in prose here since it is not part of
the committed test/tool surface) ran with `PADDLE_REMOTE_OPT_IN` set ONLY in that command's own
environment — never exported for the shell session. `PADDLE_REMOTE_CUSTOMER_DATA_OPT_IN` was never
set. The final `status` after `stop`/`tunnel-down` confirmed `probe.available: false` (worker
process gone) and `tunnel_running: false` — nothing from this run was left running, locally or
remotely.

**The end-to-end figure is the LINK, not the engine.** Inference is 0.34 s and the page takes 18.7 s.
Measured directly, three times, with incompressible bytes and no worker involved:

| direction | measurement |
|---|---|
| upload, 10 MiB by `scp` | 132.9 s → **77 KB/s** |
| upload, 2 MiB by `scp`, twice | 44.7 s and 41.2 s → **46 and 50 KB/s** |
| download, 10 MiB by `scp` | 7.5 s → 1,361 KB/s |
| bare SSH session setup | 2.7 s · 3.0 s · 4.5 s |

The workload is upload-heavy (338 KB up, 12 KB down per page), so the asymmetry falls entirely on us. The
machine was otherwise idle when measured (load average 0.15 across 16 cores, GPU at 2 MiB, every other
service stopped), so this is the path, not contention. Projected over the three Phase 2.3 populations
(6,360 pages): **≈ 33 h wall clock here against ≈ 2 h on the 2026-09-11 machine**. Recorded so that the
next wave session picks an instance on its published UPLOAD figure, not only on its GPU.

## Lossless transport experiment (2026-09-15)

Gustavo requested transfer optimization while retaining the configured instance. Its effective SSH
compression was `no`; the configured host is reached by IP. No customer bytes left the computer in
this experiment, no OCR ran, and the remote process wrote no files.

**Local sizing:** eight retained successful pages per modality, selected in hash/path order, were
wrapped in the client's Base64/JSON shape and compressed with gzip level 6. Decompression restored
the complete original JSON and PNG bytes in every case. Request bytes decreased by 29.89% for digital,
29.16% for mixed, and 26.36% for scanned pages. This selected sample is a sizing proxy for SSH's zlib,
not a measurement of network time or of pages whose earlier extraction failed.

**Synthetic link A/B:** one generated ledger page produced a PNG of 637,530 bytes and a JSON request
of 850,136 bytes. Four separate SSH command/stdin transfers used the same payload in off/on/on/off
order. The remote process returned only length, hash and read duration; all four payloads matched.
Both compressed trials negotiated `zlib@openssh.com`.

| trial | SSH compression | end-to-end seconds | remote stream-read seconds |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | off | 22.692 | 17.067 |
| 2 | on | 31.985 | 25.432 |
| 3 | on | 19.370 | 15.283 |
| 4 | off | 41.546 | 36.601 |

Mean end-to-end duration was 32.119 seconds without compression and 25.678 seconds with it, about
20% shorter in this small experiment. The large spread limits the conclusion: each trial includes a
fresh SSH setup, whereas the wave uses a persistent tunnel and forwarded HTTP. This does not establish
a 20% wave improvement or a reliable completion-time forecast. Real session wall time remains the test.

Durable private evidence: `discovery_reports/train13-logs/p23wave/closure-20260915/transport-size-audit.log`
and `synthetic-ssh-transfer.log`, both `EXIT=0`; the corresponding reproducible Python drivers are in
the parent `p23wave` directory. The implementation is W `7897518`; its targeted tests passed before
this record was written. No production OCR identity changed.

**Telemetry units:** the historical wave `bytes_up` field records raw PNG lengths before Base64 and
transport compression. `bytes_down` is a JSON reserialization estimate. W's report now labels these
bases explicitly and sets `transport_bytes_measured=False`; neither total is an encrypted-wire counter.

### Concurrent transfer follow-up (same day)

Two bounded, synthetic-only experiments used the same 850,136-byte request and serial/parallel/
parallel/serial batches, two requests per batch. Exact length and SHA-256 were verified for every
request. Neither experiment invoked OCR, sent customer data or wrote remote files.

| transport | serial seconds, four requests | parallel seconds, four requests | observed reduction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Separate compressed SSH command connections | 116.991 | 59.459 | 49.18% |
| HTTP over one persistent compressed SSH tunnel | 43.043 | 41.084 | 4.55% |

The first result includes separate connection setup and congestion state. It does not transfer to
the application's shared tunnel. The second used an ephemeral loopback HTTP checksum server and
the committed tunnel command, with one full-size warm-up (10.861 seconds) excluded from both totals.
All nine payloads in that experiment were exact. Compression negotiation was confirmed; the tunnel
and remote server controller were stopped and reaped. The first HTTP attempt was invalid: the
diagnostic did not drain verbose SSH stderr and filled its Windows pipe. It timed out before the
warm-up completed. That failed log is preserved; continuous draining fixed the instrument.

The shared-tunnel result does not justify adding concurrent requests to the OCR rung. The worker
already serializes inference, but request overlap would require new ordering, failure-drain, retry
and image-decoding concurrency proofs. The bounded live SLICE continuation therefore enables only
lossless SSH compression in its child environment and retains serial page processing. This comparison
measures synthetic transfer, not production OCR throughput or a remaining-wave completion time.

Evidence: `discovery_reports/train13-logs/p23transport-prep/parallel-upload-probe.log` and
`discovery_reports/train13-logs/p23wave/closure-20260915/persistent-http-transfer-drained.log`, both
`EXIT=0`. W at `7897518` has now passed 123 targeted tests, all 24 mutation rows (11 unaffected
historical kills retained), the full suite (9,929 passed, 48 skipped, 39 deselected, zero failed),
and 277 guards. Its live retention proof and final report remain outstanding.
